anchors.text: Fig. 1. A,B: PLGA scaffolds. These PLGA scaffolds were fabricated using a modified version of solvent merging/particulate leaching method. The PLGA scaffolds were three dimensional discs with high porosity. The height and width of the scaffold was 6 and 3 mm, respectively. The PLGA scaffolds were ready for cell seeding after sterilization by sequential replacements of ethanol overnight. Scale bar = 2 mm. C,D: SEM micrographs of the middle section of a PLGA scaffold. The approximate porosity of the scaffold was 85% according to the proportion of NaCl within a PLGA scaffold. The average range of the pore sizes of scaffolds was 80–240 μm. No residual NaCl particle was observed on the surfaces or inside the pores within the PLGA scaffolds. The porous PLGA scaffolds were well fabricated with well-mixed PLGA and NaCl particles using the solvent merging/particulate leaching method. Left (C): 800 ×; right (D): 1000 ×. Scale bar = 10 μm.

Fig. 2. Schematic of the integration system. Cells and scaffolds were placed into the inner base seats of these three bioreactors for PEMF stimulation with different exposure time. The treatment coils covered the outside of bioreactors and within the solenoids, magnetic fields of 0.13, 0.24, and 0.32 mT were generated by the PEMF stimulator. [The color figure for this article is available online at www.interscience.wiley.com.]

Fig. 3. Light micrographs of H&E-stained osteoblasts seeded onto PLGA scaffolds in PEMF-2 h group. From left to right, the osteoblasts were cultured on PLGA scaffolds for (A) 6 h, (B) 6 days, and (C) 12 days, respectively. The magnetic intensity was 0.13 mT. A,C: Scale bar = 100 μm, magnification = 100×. B: Scale bar = 200 μm, magnification = 200×. [The color figure for this article is available online at www.interscience.wiley.com.]

Fig. 6. Number of osteoblasts cultured in PLGA scaffolds with/without PEMF stimulation (0.32 mT) at 0, 6, 12, and 18 days. Six sectioned pieces of Cell/PLGA scaffolds, which were derived from two complete ones, were harvested from the same chamber of each bioreactor at each time point during the culture. PEMF-treated groups exhibited significantly less osteoblast proliferation than the control group at each time point, especially at day 18. This indicates that 0.32-mT PEMF stimulation inhibited DNA synthesis ( $ ^{*}P < 0.05 $;  $ ^{**}P < 0.01 $;  $ ^{***}P < 0.005 $).

Fig. 7. ALP activity of osteoblasts cultured in PLGA scaffolds with/without PEMF stimulation (0.13 mT) at 0, 6, 12, and 18 days. The supernatant ($n=6$) was harvested from the same chamber of each bioreactor at each time point during the culture and data were expressed as mean $\pm$ SD. The ALP activity in PEMF-treated groups were significantly lower than the control group. However, PEMF-2 h reached the highest ALP activity at the end of culture period compared to others ($P<0.05$; $P<0.01$; $P<0.005$).

Fig. 8. ALP activity of osteoblasts cultured in PLGA scaffolds with/without PEMF stimulation (0.24 mT) at 0, 6, 12, and 18 days. The supernatant ($n=6$) was harvested from the same chamber of each bioreactor at each time point during the culture and data were expressed as mean $\pm$ SD. PEMF-2 h had similar ALP activity compared to the control group during the early and middle stages of the culture, followed by an increase at day 18. PEMF-8 h showed a decrease of ALP activity at day 12, but later had the highest ALP activity at the late stages of the culture ($^\circ$P < 0.05); $^\circ$P < 0.01).

Fig. 9. ALP activity of osteoblasts cultured in PLGA scaffolds with/ without PEMF stimulation (0.32 mT) at 0, 6, 12, and 18 days. The supernatant ($n=6$) was harvested from the same chamber of each bioreactor at each time point during the culture and data were expressed as mean $\pm$ SD. The ALP activity in all groups increased over time. Moreover, PEMF-8 h had the highest ALP activity compared to the control and PEMF-2 h at each time point during the culture period. PEMF-2 h also showed higher ALP activity than the control during the early and middle stages of the culture ($P<0.05$; $P<0.01$; $P<0.005$).

Fig. 5. Number of osteoblasts cultured in PLGA scaffolds with/without PEMF stimulation (0.24 mT) at 0, 6, 12, and 18 days. Six sectioned pieces of Cell/PLGA scaffolds, which were derived from two complete ones, were harvested from the same chamber of each bioreactor at each time point during the culture. The cell number of each group was similar during the period of culture except at day 18, when it was significantly lower in both PEMF-treated groups than in the control group ( $ ^{**}P < 0.01 $).

In this system, multi-channel EMG signals generated by diverse hand motions are collected by an ionic hydrogel electrode array and processed by a trained CNN to recognize corresponding hand motions, which are then transmitted to VR Unity platform to synchronize the virtual hand movement. This setup enables the hand injury patient wearing a VR headset, to perform hand motions and experience real-time feedback in the virtual space, realizing VR hand rehabilitation. Figure 1(b) shows that the prepared ionic hydrogel comprises branched polyethylene imine

Figure 2 Electrical, mechanical, and adhesive properties of the ionic hydrogel. (a) EIS plots of the ionic hydrogels with different contents of LiCl. (b) Conductivity of the ionic hydrogels with different contents of LiCl calculated from the EIS plots. (c) Stress-strain curves of the ionic hydrogels with different LiCl contents. (d) Strain elongation of the ionic hydrogels as a function of LiCl content. (e) Adhesion force curves of the ionic hydrogels with different LiCl contents to dry porcine skin. (f) Corresponding adhesion forces of the ionic hydrogels to dry porcine skin as a function of LiCl content. (g) Adhesion forces of the ionic hydrogel to different substrates in dry and wet conditions, including glass, Cu, PET, pig skin, PMMA, PS, PTFE, and rubber. (h) Adhesion force curves of the ionic hydrogel's repetitive adhesion test for 8 cycles. (i) Optical microscope images of the gap of the break ionic hydrogel before and after self-healing. (j) and (k) Stress-strain curves and self-healing efficiency of the original and self-healed ionic hydrogels with different healing times.

Figure 3 Electrophysiological signals monitoring of the ionic hydrogel electrode. (a) Raw EEG signals of a testing subject in mental states of gritting teeth, blinking, and smiling. (b) Corresponding time-frequency spectrograms of different EEG signals. (c) FFT results extracted from the raw EEG signals. (d) ECG signals acquired by the ionic hydrogel and commercial Ag/AgCl gel electrodes under different vibration intensities. (e) Corresponding signal-to-noise ratio of the ECG signals acquired by ionic hydrogel and commercial electrodes. (f) Continuous ECG signals of a young man monitored by the ionic hydrogel for over 60 s. (g) EMG signals acquired by the ionic hydrogel during dry and sweaty skin conditions. (h) EMG signals acquired by the ionic hydrogel with varying clenching forces. (i) EMG signals acquired by the ionic hydrogel for different hand motions including grasping, moving objects, and drawing a line. (j) EMG signals from the ionic hydrogel in normal state and after its self-healing.

Figure 4 CNN-assisted hand motion recognition using the ionic hydrogel electrodes array. (a) Photographs of 14 hand gestures according to the Jebsen hand function test. (b) 6-channel raw EMG signals of one volunteer for the 14 Jebsen hand gestures. (c) Schematic illustration for structure of the constructed CNN model. (d) Confusion matrix result for the CNN training of 5600 EMG signal data sets. (e) Distribution of the initial data before training in a 2D space. (f) Distribution of the datasets after training in a 2D space.

Figure 5 VR hand rehabilitation system for hand injury patients. (a) Sketch illustrating the process flow of the VR hand rehabilitation system. (b) Overview of the logic of the EMG hand motion recognition assisted by the CNN model. (c)-(f) Photographs of a participant wearing a VR headset while performing the four hand motions including grasping a cup, moving a cup, pinching cards, and flipping cards. (g)-(j) 6-channel real-time EMG signals corresponding to the left four hand gestures.

Figure 1. Nrf2/ARE signaling was activated in articular cartilage of patients with OA
Cartilage from OA patients and healthy donors was processed for lysate preparation or RNA
isolation using method described in method section. (A) Protein expression of Nrf2 and its
signaling target HO-1 and SOD2 was investigated by immunoblotting using antibodies
against indicated protein. β-actin was used as a control for equal loading. Fold change
relative to β-actin for the expression these proteins were quantified by measuring specific
signal intensities using ImageJ software. Immunoblot results are representatives of three
blots performed on samples obtained from three individuals. *p 0.05, as compared to
normal cartilage. (B) Expression of Nrf2, HO-1 and SOD2 was measured by quantitative
PCR using SYBR® green assay (Life Technologies). β-actin was used as endogenous
expression control. (C–E) RNA was isolated from damaged or smooth cartilage for same
patients and mRNA levels of (C) Nrf2, (D) HO-1 and (E) SOD2 were determined by
SYBR® green assay (Life Technologies). Each symbol represents a single patient and
horizontal lines shows the mean value of expression levels in the indicated number of
samples. Bar graph represents mean±SD from three subjects. *p 0.05, as compared to
normal cartilage or smooth cartilage.
Figure 2. Nrf2/ARE signaling was activated in human OA chondrocytes under pathological conditions
Figure 2. Nrf2/ARE signaling was activated in human OA chondrocytes under pathological conditions
Figure 3. Oxidative stress was enhanced in human OA chondrocytes under pathological conditions
Figure 4. Nrf2 over-expression in OA chondrocytes inhibited oxidative stress while its deficiency intensified the oxidative stress under pathological conditions
Figure 5. Nrf2 over-expression inhibited apoptosis in OA chondrocytes under pathological conditions
Figure 6. Nrf2 over-expression inhibited both extrinsic and intrinsic apoptotic pathways in OA chondrocytes under pathological conditions
Figure 7. Nrf2 over-expression activated ERK1/2 signaling in human OA chondrocytes under pathological conditions
Figure 8. Schematic representation of proposed mechanism of Nrf2/ARE mediated protective effects in human OA chondrocytes

Human OA chondrocytes were transfected with siRNA specific for Nrf2 (siNrf2, 100 nM) or negative controls siRNA (siCNT, 100 nM) using X-tremeGENE™ siRNA transfection reagent or transfected with Nrf2 expression plasmid (pNrf2, 1μg) or pcDNA3.1 as control plasmid (1μg) using P3 Primary Cell 4D-Nucleofector™ X Kit on 4D on Amaxa Nucleofection System. (A, B) Forty-eight hours after the transfection with (A) siRNA or (B) expression vector, OA chondrocytes were stained with DHR123 (5 μM) for 0.5 h at 37°C, and stimulated with IL-1β (1 ng/ml) for 30 minutes at 37°C and ROS generation was estimated by measuring fluorescence emission at 535 nm. Bar graph shows arbitrary fluorescence units indicating ROS levels. (C–D) Forty-eight hours after the transfection with (C) siRNA or (D) expression vector, OA chondrocytes were stained with IL-1β (1 ng/ml) for 30 minutes at 37°C, supernatants were collected and generation of H₂O₂ in the supernatant was estimated using Amplex red assay as described in method section. Data points represent mean±SD of three replicates from a representative experiment and three such independent experiments were carried out.*p 0.05, as compared to control, # 0.05, as compared to IL-1β.

Human OA chondrocytes were transfected with Nrf2 expression plasmid (pNrf2, 1μg) or pcDNA3.1 as control plasmid (1μg) using P3 Primary Cell 4D-Nucleofector™ X Kit on 4D on Amaxa Nucleofection System. Forty-eight hours after the transfection, OA chondrocytes were serum starved and then stimulated with or without IL-1β (10 ng/ml) for 48 h. (A). At end of treatment, cell lysates were prepared using RIPA buffer and protein levels of cleaved caspase-3, cleaved caspase-8, pro-caspase-9, cleaved PARP and Bid were investigated by immunoblotting using antibodies against indicated protein. β-actin was used as a control for equal loading. Immunoblot results are representatives of three blots performed on samples obtained from three individuals. (B) Fold change relative to β-actin for the expression of these proteins were quantified by measuring specific signal intensities using ImageJ software. *p 0.05, as compared to pcDNA, # 0.05, as compared to pcDNA+IL-1β. (C) After transfection, OA chondrocyte were stimulated IL-1β (1 ng/ml) for 30 minutes at 37°C and then stained with JC-1 (2.5 μM) and mitochondrial membrane potential loss was measured by ratio of red to green fluorescence. Values were expressed relative to unstimulated control and graph shows mean ± SD of four replicates from a representative experiment and three such independent experiments were carried out. *p 0.05, as compared to control, # 0.05, as compared to IL-1β. (D) Cytosolic lysates were prepared after 48 h of IL-1β (10 ng/ml) stimulation in transfected chondrocytes and levels of cytosolic cytochrome-c was estimated by immunoblotting using validated antibody. β-actin was used as a control for equal loading. Immunoblot results are representatives of three blots performed on samples obtained from three individuals.

Human OA chondrocytes were transfected with Nrf2 expression plasmid (pNrf2, 1μg) or pcDNA3.1 as control plasmid (1μg) using P3 Primary Cell 4D-Nucleofector™ X Kit on 4D on Amaxa Nucleofection System. Forty-eight hours after the transfection, OA chondrocytes were serum starved and then stimulated with or without IL-1β (10 ng/ml) for 15 and 30 minutes at 37°C (A–C). At end of treatment, cell lysates were prepared using RIPA buffer and immunoblotting was performed to detect the protein levels of (A) p-ERK1/2 (Thr180/Tyr182), total ERK1/2, p-MEK1/2 (Ser217/221), total MEK1/2, p-ELK-1 (Ser383), p-P70S6K (Ser411), p-P90RSK (Ser380). β-actin was used as a control for equal loading. Immunoblot results are representatives of three blots performed on samples obtained from three individuals. (B–C) At end of transfection, chondrocytes were treated with ERK inhibitor PD98059 (30 μM) for 2 h and then stimulated with IL-1β (10 ng/ml) for (B) 15 minutes and (C) 16 h at 37°C and processed for (B) immunoblotting with p-ERK1/2 and total ERK1/2 and (C) TUNEL assay as described in method section. Bar graph shows mean ±SD of three replicates from a representative experiment and three independent experiments were carried out. *p 0.05, as compared to pcDNA, # 0.05, as compared to pcDNA+IL-1β, $ 0.05, as compared to pNrf2+IL-1β.

anchors.text: Fig. 1. The production process and the role of 3D printed scaffolds. (Created in https://BioRender.com).
Fig. 2. Overview of the 3D printing scaffolds for articular cartilage/osteochondral regeneration. (Created in https://BioRender.com).

Fig. 3. Schematic of articular cartilage composition and inflammation mechanisms. (A) Schematic diagram of articular synovial fluid and its boundary layer, showing the distribution of linear hyaluronic acid (HA, gray), mucin glycoprotein lubricin (purple), phospholipids (monolayer, green; bilayer, blue) on the collagen network (orange) [44]. Copyright 2022, ACS Publications. (B) A variety of inflammatory pathways and mechanisms may be involved in the pathogenesis of osteoarthritis. In this model, injury or overuse, often in the context of other risk factors, triggers local tissue damage, failed tissue repair, and a vicious cycle of chronic inflammation in the joint involving a variety of molecular components and mechanisms. Such chronic inflammation leads to or mediates the progressive loss of cartilage, pain, and joint dysfunction. CPB, carboxypeptidase B; DAMPs, damage-associated molecular patterns; NO, nitric oxide [45]. Copyright 2016, Springer Nature. (C) Microstructure of normal and damaged osteochondral units. The osteochondral unit is composed of articular cartilage (hyaline and calcified cartilage) and subchondral bone (subchondral bone plate and subarticular spongiosa). The boundaries between these regions are the tidemark, which separates the deep zone of hyaline articular cartilage from the calcified cartilage region, and the cement line, which demarcates the calcified cartilage region from the underlying subchondral bone plate. (Created in https://BioRender.com).

Fig. 4. Schematic diagrams of various 3D printing methods. Schematic diagrams of various 3D bioprinting techniques. (A) Inkjet printing: Droplets of bioink-cell mixtures are formed using thermal or piezoelectric drivers. (B) Extrusion printing: A continuous bioink filament is extruded via pneumatic, piston, or screw forces. (C) Freeform reversible embedding printing: Bioink is extruded into a reversible support bath to create support-free structures. (D) Digital light processing printing: Photopolymers are cured in a container with ultraviolet or visible light for layer-by-layer 3D model fabrication [71]. Copyright 2021, Theranostics. Schematic of low-temperature vertical 3D cryogenic (bio)printing. (E) GelMA-based hydrogels form interconnected gradient and non-uniform microchannels along the vertical axis under directional freezing. (F) Vertical and various -angle 3D cryogenic (bio)printing of hydrogel filament arrays. (G) Multimaterial vertical 3D cryogenic (bio)printing of single and hydrogel filament array hydrogel filaments [72]. Copyright 2022, Wiley. (H) Response process of 4D- printed scaffolds. From left to right: printing, dissolving, light, magnetism and temperature changes over time, and potential for vascularized bone regeneration. (I) and (J) Printing processes of 4D and 5D printing [73]. Copyright 2023, Springer.

Fig. 5. Strategies to strengthen scaffolds' mechanical properties and relevant experimental evidence. (A) The importance of scaffold mechanical strength and its partial modification measures. (Created in https://BioRender.com) Features of 3D printed layered scaffolds. (B) Anatomical images of 3D printed layered scaffolds; (C) Rough image of three regions; (D) Images of three areas under light microscopy; (E) SEM image of the scaffold in the side view; (F) The string size of each region in the scaffold; (G) Pore size of each region in the scaffold; (H) Maximum force of layered scaffolds in each region; (I) Extension of layered scaffolds in each region under maximum force. Quantitative analysis of (J) COL II expression levels, (K) COL X expression levels, (L) chondrogenic gene Sox-9, and (M) chondrogenic gene Aggrecan in co-cultures of chondrocytes and bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells at varying ratios. (*p < 0.05, **p < 0.01, ***p < 0.001) [139]. Copyright 2023, Elsevier. (N-Q) In vivo osteochondral regeneration. The results of Hematoxylin - Eosin staining (NO) and Toluidine blue staining (PQ) both indicated that the DE-loaded graded scaffold significantly promoted the regeneration of cartilage and subchondral bone. The area between the red arrows indicates the location of the osteochondral defect [75]. Copyright 2024, Elsevier.

Fig. 7. Schematic of osteochondral scaffold manufacturing and its therapeutic efficacy. (A) In an in vivo rat osteochondral defect model, pre- gel solutions of bone and cartilage layers were sequentially injected and polymerized in situ. A relatively high concentration of KGN promotes chondrogenesis of recruited BMSCs, while low- concentration KGN synergizes with  $ \beta $-TCP to induce osteogenesis of BMSCs [151]. Copyright 2023, Wiley. (B) 3D- printed bilayer Bi-Hydrogel - Exos scaffolds with specific microenvironments promote physiological regeneration of critical- sized osteochondral defects in rats via sustained bioactive vesicle release from a double- network hydrogel system [18]. Copyright 2023, Wiley. (C) Schematic representation of 3D-printed scaffolds implanted in rat knee cartilage defects. (D) Representative MRI scans and 3D- reconstructed micro- CT images of cartilage regeneration at 6 and 12 weeks post- surgery, with arrows indicating defect locations. They show subchondral bone regeneration in different experimental groups: sham control (CTRL), hydrogel, biohydrogel, and biohydrogel - exosome scaffold implants [18]. Copyright 2023, Wiley. Macroscopic images and micro- CT analysis results of repaired osteochondral defects in four groups at 6 weeks post- surgery. (E) Macroscopic images of repaired osteochondral defects in different groups. (F) 3D- reconstructed micro- CT images and (G) coronal and sagittal sections of repaired joints. Black circles indicate original defect boundaries. Red areas represent highly mineralized bone tissue, and yellow areas indicate new bone [151]. Copyright 2023, Wiley. Quantitative data based on micro- CT images for four groups: (H) BV/TV, (I) Tb.N, (J) Tb.Sp, and (K) Tb.Th. Four different BLH groups were used: control group (C/O, upper cartilage layer with CLH/KGN(-) and lower bone layer with OLH/ $ \beta $-TCP(-)/KGN(-)), group with both layers containing KGN but no  $ \beta $-TCP (C-K/O-K, upper cartilage layer with CLH/KGN(+) and lower bone layer with OLH/ $ \beta $-TCP(-)/KGN(+)), group with only lower layer containing  $ \beta $-TCP but no KGN (C/O-T, upper cartilage layer with CLH/KGN(-)) and lower bone layer with OLH/ $ \beta $-TCP(+)/KGN(-)), and group with both KGN and  $ \beta $-TCP embedded (C-K/O-TK, upper cartilage layer with CLH/KGN(+) and lower bone layer with OLH/ $ \beta $-TCP(-)/KGN(+) [151]). Copyright 2023, Wiley.

Fig. 8. The function of smart scaffolds in controlling the release of active substances and their therapeutic efficacy. (A) Schematic diagram showing the presence of the printed scaffold in the body of tumor-bearing nude mice after ultrasound irradiation [80]. Copyright 2024, Elsevier. (B) The hierarchical scaffold incorporating DE significantly stimulates the regeneration of hyaline cartilage and subchondral bone through the release of Si ions from DE microparticles [75]. Copyright 2024, Elsevier. The Stent Promotes Chondrocyte Maturation and Osteogenic Differentiation of rBMSCs. (C) CLSM images demonstrating COL II expression in chondrocytes cultured on scaffolds for 3 days (Blue: DAPI nuclear counterstaining; Green: FITC-phalloidin cytoskeletal staining; Red: COL II immunostaining). (D) ALP histochemical staining results of rBMSCs cultured on scaffolds for 14 days. (E) ARS staining of rBMSCs cultured on scaffolds for 21 days. Compared with GelMA scaffolds, chondrocytes cultured on 5DE and 10DE scaffolds exhibited significantly enhanced COL II protein expression, confirming the superior efficacy of DE scaffolds in promoting chondrocyte maturation. Furthermore, qualitative analyses of ALP and ARS staining demonstrated that the incorporation of DE microparticles facilitated osteogenic differentiation of rBMSCs [75]. Copyright 2024, Elsevier. (F) In vitro chondrogenesis assessment of IPN and S-IPN constructs with TGF-β3 in culture medium or constructs. Histochemical and immunohistochemical staining for sGAG, collagen, calcium, type I, II and X collagen at day 21 and 42 [202]. Copyright 2021, Elsevier. (GH) The release profile of TGF-β3 from the constructs was assessed using an ELISA assay over the first 3 days and up to 21 days post-culture. n = 4, α, β, ε, γ = Statistical significance was determined by two-way ANOVA with S-IPN and 1% alginate, 1% alginate/sulfated alginate, 10% GelMA, and IPN [202]. Copyright 2021, Elsevier. (I) Demonstrate the release of CS and HA from the bilayer PGHc-PGPH scaffold when immersed in PBS, with and without ultrasound irradiation, over different durations [80]. Copyright 2024, Elsevier.

Fig. 9. Images of in vivo experiments with scaffolds. (A) Show the location of transplanting biphasic constructs made from chondrogenic or osteogenic composite spheroids. Growth factor-stem cell hybrids formed each type of spheroid, which were layered in 3D-printed microwells to create biphasic layers. These biphasic constructs were then transplanted into subchondral bone defects for in vivo analysis [179]. Copyright 2022, Wiley. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) images of chondrocytes cultured on PU(B), PU-GG(C), PU-GG-HA(D), PU-GG-GA(E), and PU-GG-HA-GA(F) scaffolds at different magnifications. (G) RT-PCR results for the expression of collagen I, collagen II, and aggrecan in chondrocytes cultured on the scaffolds on day 7 (values are mean ± SD, n = 3, P < 0.05). Statistical significance between the control and other samples for the same gene expression is indicated by ( $ \uparrow $P < 0.05). Numerical symbols indicate significant differences compared to the PU scaffold ( $ \neq $P < 0.05) [215]. Copyright 2022, Elsevier. (H) Chondrogenesis of BMSCs in diverse hydrogels. Histological and histochemical staining (H&E, Alcian blue/nuclear fast red, and immunohistochemical staining for collagen types II, I, and X) of frozen cartilage sections. Scale bar, 100  $ \mu $m [17]. Copyright 2023, Elsevier. (I) In vitro differentiation of stem cells within biphasic construct. Col1a IHC staining of vertically sectioned BS/TS (scale bar = 200  $ \mu $m), and Col2a IHC staining of vertically cross-sectioned BS/TS (scale bar = 200  $ \mu $m) (Area 1: cells spread from BS, Area 2: cells near the borderline, Area 3: cells spread from TS) [179]. Copyright 2022, Wiley.

Fig. 10. Assessment of stent biomechanics and bone regeneration. (A) 3D model reconstruction images of the scaffold; (B) SEM images and EBSD images of the scaffold. Biomechanical Analysis Based on Finite Element Analysis: (C) The finite element models demonstrate stress distribution patterns in fracture fragments, femoral shaft, plate, screws, cement particles, and scaffolds under compressive loading applied to either the distal unilateral condyle (a) or the entire articular surface (b). From left to right, the four models correspond to the blank model, cement model, Stent Model, and Stent II model, respectively. (D) von Mises values across different anatomical regions under distinct loading modes (FF: Fracture Fragment, FS: Femoral Shaft, S/C: Stent or Cement particles). (E) Anteroposterior and lateral radiographs of different groups at 6, 12, 24, and 48 weeks postoperatively. (F) Continuous micro-CT images in the sagittal and axial planes of different groups at 6, 12, 24, and 48 weeks postoperatively (yellow arrows indicate the defect area, red arrows indicate the implanted scaffold, and green arrows indicate newly regenerated bone. The results of radiographs, micro-CTs, MRIs, and histological analyses are from the same rabbit model). (G) MOCART scores in different groups at 6, 12, 24, and 48 weeks post- surgery [25]. Copyright 2024, Elsevier.

Fig. 11. The role and therapeutic effect of scaffolds in animal experiments. Meniscal repair using PZG and PZG-DS/KGN scaffolds in a porcine model. (A) Intraoperative images of meniscal repair in the porcine model (scale bar: 1 cm). (B) MRI images of the knee joint in the menisectomy, PZG, and PZG-DS/KGN groups (scale bar: 1 cm). (C) Macroscopic observations [15]. Copyright 2023, Wiley. (D) Schematic diagram of the function of anisotropic scaffolds and their application in animal models. (Created in https://BioRender.com/) (E) The process of implanting pl - PNASC and pl - PNASC/PNAGA meniscal scaffolds in a rabbit model: (i) incise skin and fascia; (ii) cut the medial collateral ligament and open the knee joint capsule; (iii) perform menisectomy; (iv) implant the meniscal scaffold; (v) suture the medial collateral ligament and close the knee joint capsule; (vi) suture the skin and fascia. (F) Macroscopic observations of femoral condyles, tibial plateaus, and meniscal scaffolds at 12 weeks post - implantation. Rabbits with only meniscal exposure were assigned to the sham - surgery group, and those with only menisectomy formed the menisectomy group. In the experimental group, pl - PNASC and pl - PNASC/PNAGA meniscal implants were transplanted into the two knees of rabbits. The positions of pl - PNASC and pl - PNASC/PNAGA meniscal scaffolds on the tibial plateau are circled with red dashed lines (scale bar: 1 cm). Histological evaluation of femoral condyles (FCs) and tibial plateaus (TPs) at 12 weeks post-implantation. (G) Histological evaluation of the femoral condyle and tibial plateau at 4, 8, and 12 weeks post - implantation. H&E: Hematoxylin and eosin staining; SOFG: Safranin O-fast green staining. (Scale bar: 500 μm). (H) OARSI (Osteoarthritis Research Society International) scoring system for cartilage degeneration assessment at 8 weeks and 12 weeks. Data are expressed as mean ± standard deviation (SD) (n = 4). Statistical significance was determined by one-way ANOVA with post hoc Bonferroni correction. *P < 0.05, **P < 0.001, ***P < 0.001, ***P < 0.0001; ns: non-significant [105]. Copyright 2024, Wiley.

Fig. 6. Experimental evidence of pore size differences in scaffolds. (A) Macroscopic appearance of 3D- printed constructs after freeze-drying and scanning electron microscope images of printed hydrogels; (B) Mean thickness and pore size values analyzed by micro- CT. (G) Metabolic activity of ATDC5 cells in 3D- bioprinted hydrogels after 1- and 7- day culture in an inflammatory environment, and (C- F) media and cytokine release into the culture medium. Data are presented as mean ± SD (*p ≤ 0.05, **p ≤ 0.01, ***p ≤ 0.001, ****p ≤ 0.0001 by non- parametric Kruskal- Wallis test) [129]. Copyright 2024, Elsevier. (H) Chondrogenesis in co- cultures of chondrocytes and bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells with different pore sizes [139]. Copyright 2023, Elsevier. (I-M) qPCR analyzed Sox9, Col2a1, Aggrecan, Col1a1, and Col10a1 gene expression in ATDC5 cells cultured on 3D printed scaffolds for 28 days. The scaffolds included critical point dried (CPD) with 200 μm pores (CPD200), freeze-dried (FD) with 700 μm pores (FD700), and FD700 with 3× more seeded cells. Results were normalized to GAPDH. The comparative ΔCT method (2^{-\Delta\Delta CT}) calculated relative transcription levels, with the highest set to 1. Statistical analysis occurred at the ΔCT level. n = 3, * indicates p < 0.05 [154]. Copyright 2021, Elsevier. (N) The relationship between compressive modulus and pore morphology of different scaffold components (PCL-only, HA15, HA30, dual-gradient). Small-pore (0.2 mm) scaffolds had a significantly higher compressive modulus than other groups, while medium-pore (0.5 mm) scaffolds were statistically similar. Single-gradient and dual-gradient scaffolds also showed similar modulus to medium-pore and large-pore scaffolds. Groups with the same letter were not statistically different (p > 0.05). Each group included n = 5 scaffolds. (O) The relationship between pore morphology and yield stress in different scaffold components (PCL-only, HA15, HA30, dual-gradient). Small-pore scaffolds had higher yield stress than other groups, with statistically significant differences (p < 0.05). Groups with the same letter were not statistically different (p > 0.05). Each group included n = 5 scaffolds. (P) The compressive modulus of all uniform (0.2 mm, 0.5 mm, 0.9 mm) scaffolds was analyzed as a continuous function of pre-compressive porosity, with the model equation log(E) = 1.27log(1 - φ) + 2.39(R^2 = 0.8698). (Q) The pre-compressive porosity of all uniform (0.2 mm, 0.5 mm, 0.9 mm) scaffolds was analyzed as a continuous function of yield stress, with the model equation log(E) = 1.37log(1 - φ) + 1.15(R^2 = 0.8057) [176]. Copyright 2019, Elsevier.

anchors.text: Fig. 1 Characterization of composite scaffold and schematic diagram of EMF device. The components of Thermo-sensitive PLGA-PEG-PLGA are Polyethylene glycol (PEG), dl-Lactide (LA) and glycolide (GA). The molecular weight of PEG is 1500. LA (113.46 g), GA (30.48 g), PEG (60 g) were reacted in the solvent of Deuterated chloroform with the internal standard tetramethylsilane. A Thermo-sensitive PLGA–PEG–PLGA copolymers exhibited a free-flowing sol at ambient temperature (25 °C) and B spontaneously converted into a semi-solid hydrogel at body temperature (36 °C). Every 100 g of HAC scaffold contains 45 g of HA and 55 g of collagen. C Macroscopic observation of cylindrical HAC scaffold produced by hydroxyapatite and collagen I. D Image of scanning electron micrograph (SEM) showing porous microstructure of HAC. E Assembly of composite scaffold. The cell-loaded aqueous sol was injected on the top of HAC and then incubated at 37 °C for 30 min. Arrow: the site BMSCs loaded. F Presentation of electromagnetic fields (EMF) device consisting of waveform generator, oscilloscope, and Helmholtz coils. Cells were stimulated at the center of coils, which was placed in an incubator at 37 °C and 5% CO₂

Fig. 3 EMF enhanced expressions of proliferation-related genes and proteins partly by activating PI3K/Akt/mTOR pathway. A Expressions of Cyclin D1, CDK4, and PCNA were significantly increased in the presence of EMF. B Results of qRT-PCR and western blot showed that EMF promoted phosphorylation of PI3K, Akt, and mTOR proteins. C PI3K inhibitor (Dactolisib) could significantly reduce the increased expression of Cyclin D1, CDK4, and PCNA induced by EMF both in gene and protein levels. D Inhibition of mTOR by AZD8055 showed results similar to those in (C). Data are shown as mean ± standard deviation (n=3). # indicates no significant difference, *p<0.05, **p<0.01, ***p<0.001 compared to the group with or without EMF as indicated

Fig. 4 Immunofluorescence analysis of chondrogenesis-associated proteins. Immunofluorescence labeling and quantitative analysis indicate that chondrogenic medium dramatically improved expressions of chondrogenesis-associated proteins (including Col2, Aggrecan, and SOX9) and EMF could further enhance their intensities. Data are shown as mean ± standard deviation (n=5). # indicates no significant difference,  $ ^{*}p<0.05 $,  $ ^{**}p<0.01 $,  $ ^{***}p<0.001 $ compared to group without EMF

Fig. 5 EMF enhanced chondrogenesis partly by activating Wnt1/LRP6/β-catenin pathway. A Expressions of Col2, Aggrecan, and SOX9 were significantly increased in the presence of EMF. B Results of qRT-PCR and western blot show that EMF activates the Wnt1/LRP6/β-catenin signaling pathway. C Wnt1 inhibitor (SM04960) significantly reduced the increased expression of Col2, Aggrecan, and SOX9 induced by EMF both in gene and protein levels. D Inhibition of β-catenin by LF3 shows results similar to those in (C). Data are shown as mean ± standard deviation (n=3). # indicates no significant difference, *p<0.05, **p<0.01, ***p<0.001 compared to group without EMF or the group as indicated

Fig. 7 Morphological and mechanical evaluation of regenerative cartilage. A Representations of osteochondral defects with different treatments. B Macroscopic observation show that osteochondral repair was improved with time from 4 to 12 weeks post implantation. Particularly, the smooth neocartilage with similar appearance to adjacent native tissue was found in EMF group. C Strain–stress curve of regenerative tissue with representative points at intervals of 0.5% strain. D The compression modulus was calculated at strain of 5% and the highest modulus in EMF group suggested excellent mechanical properties. Data are shown as mean ± standard deviation (n=5). # indicates no significant difference, *p<0.05, **p<0.01, ***p<0.001 compared to the group as indicated

Fig. 8 Micro-CT analysis for subchondral bone regeneration. A Reconstructed images of surfaces (first line) and defect area (second line) show improved repair incrementally in groups from left to right. B Quantitative analysis of micro-CT data further confirms that bone volume per total volume (BV/TV) and bone mineral density (BMD) were both incrementally increased in groups from left to right, in terms of trabecular volume of interest (VOI) and cartilage and cortical (C&C) VOI. The values of BV/TV and BMD were highest in the EMF group. Data are shown as mean ± standard deviation (n=5). # indicates no significant difference, *p<0.05, **p<0.01, ***p<0.001 compared to the group as indicated.

Fig. 10 Histological scores for evaluation of osteochondral repair. A Scores for overall defect evaluation. B Scores for subchondral bone evaluation. C Scores for cartilage evaluation. Compared to the Blank group, scores for all parameters except bone morphology were significantly higher in the EMF group. Data are shown as median (inter quartile range (IQR)) (n=5). # indicates no significant difference, *p<0.05, **p<0.01, ***p<0.001 compared to blank group. The bold horizontal indicates no significant difference among groups under its coverage.

Fig. 11 Immunohistochemical staining for evaluation of chondrogenesis- and osteogenesis-related proteins. A Positive staining of Col2, Aggrecan, and Col X was evident in cell-loaded groups, while there were almost no positive cells in the first three groups without BMSCs. The EMF group showed the strongest staining of Col2 and Aggrecan proteins. The Col X expression in EMF group was relatively lower compared to the "HAC + gel + MSC" group. B Osteocalcin (OCN) and Col1 were visualized in the last three groups, and their staining was remarkably stronger compared to other two groups. The number of cells positively expressing OCN or Col1 was relatively higher in the EMF group than those in "HAC + gel" and "HAC + gel + MSC" groups. (C) RNA expression of Col2, Aggrecan, Col X, OCN and Col1 in regenerated tissue was measured by RT-PCR. The HAC + gel + MSC + EMF group showed highest level of Col2, Aggrecan, Col X, OCN and Col1 relative RNA expression, and significantly higher than any other groups. The magnification of immunohistochemical staining pictures are 3X for upper rows and 30X for lower rows. Data are shown as mean ± standard deviation (n = 5). *p < 0.05, **p < 0.01, ***p < 0.001 compared to blank group

Fig. 5. Generalization ability based on original features (A) and regular-added feature (B) of different algorithms for viscosity, fitting ability (C) based on original features and regular-added feature of different algorithms for viscosity.

Fig. 7A and B also show the results for the two different input feature sets. It was found that regular-added feature gave rise to an overall decrease in  $ R^2 $, but improved the prediction stability of the model. This implies that regular-added feature, although sacrifices some prediction accuracy, enhances the model's stability. In general, the RF algorithm offers the best performance when using the original features. The fitting ability of the different models is shown in Fig. 7C. The results concerning model accuracy and the effect of regular-added feature are in agreement with the previous viscosity prediction. This consistency is due to the inherent functional relationship existing between shear stress and viscosity, leading to similar fitting performance. Except for the RF model, the rest of algorithms perform poorly in predicting high shear stress levels. Specifically, the MLP and XGBoost models tend to overpredict data points with experimental shear stress greater than  $ 2 \times 10^2 $ Pa, with predicted shear stress clustering at  $ 4 \times 10^2 $ and  $ 8 \times 10^2 $ Pa. This overprediction may be due to increased nonlinearity in experimental shear stresses exceeding  $ 2 \times 10^2 $ Pa.

anchors.text: Fig. 1. Schematic representation of two principal modes of ESPC mobilization, migration and recruitment (illustrations not to scale) in response to guidance gradients (e.g., chemokines and growth factors). (A) In general, ESPCs can mobilize from a central cell niche (e.g., bone marrow), disseminate throughout the body via the blood flow, recognize and interact with microvascular endothelial cells in desired tissues or organs, where these cells replenish the local niches during homeostasis or reach the sites of injury, and participate in tissue regeneration. (B) The second mode of ESPC mobilization, which is known as interstitial migration, requires that stem/progenitor cells migrate within the extracellular matrix, recognize and obey extravascular guidance gradients to reach the injured site and participate in tissue regeneration. In contrast to mode (A), this trafficking mode occurs independently of blood flow and requires active amoeboid movement.

Fig. 2. PMRs of joint-resident ESPCs in cartilage regeneration and repair. The full line represents the short-distance PMRs, whereas the dotted line represents long-distance PMRs. In adults, BM-MSCs can directly contribute to the regeneration of full-thickness cartilage injuries. However, how BM-MSCs can migrate to the superficial AC remains unclear. In addition, the direct migration of SD-MSCs, SF-MSCs and CSPCs to the sites of superficial cartilage defects has been experimentally confirmed. IFP-SCs might be recruited to the synovial lining and the synovial fluid for the regeneration of cartilage injury. Furthermore, the PMR of Rg-MSCs along the perichondrium in rabbit knee joints has been explored.

Fig. 3. Representation of the anti-inflammatory, immunomodulatory and regenerative effects (including anti-apoptotic, pro-anabolic, secretory and chondrogenic effects) of ESPCs. ESCPs can regulate immune cells through direct cell-to-cell contact and the secretion of anti-inflammatory cytokines (A). ESPCs also play a pivotal role in metabolism regulation by inhibiting chondrocyte apoptosis and fibrosis, enhancing their viability and promoting ECM secretion (B). In addition, ESPCs can differentiate into chondrocytes and secrete various bioactive factors to modulate tissue function and communicate with local stimuli through autocrine and paracrine signaling (C).

Fig. 4. Conceptual framework depicting the cellular and/or tissue activity responses to acute cartilage injury. Catabolic and anabolic processes are involved in the response to injury and overlap with one another. The early phase (within the first 3-5 days) is characterized by inflammation, cell death/apoptosis, and matrix degradation. This phase is followed by the intermediate phase (for 1 week), which involves initiation of the anabolic responses and abatement of the catabolic responses. Subsequently, the third limited remodeling/matrix formation phase (10–14 days post injury) gradually dominates, and this phase might last longer.

Fig. 5. Scaffold-based drug delivery systems (SDDSs), including covalent (A) and noncovalent (B-D) binding, and their release profiles for cartilage regeneration. (A) Covalently bound chemoattractants attached by covalent linkers to the carrier matrix. (B) Physical absorption of chemoattractants through physicochemical interactions to the spongy matrix (e.g., collagen, gelatin or silk fibroin). (C) Physical entrapment of chemoattractants in hydrogel (C-1) and microscaffolds/electrospinning (C-2). (D) Ion complexation of chemoattractants with an oppositely charged matrix.

Fig. 6. Future perspectives regarding endogenous cell recruitment strategies for in situ AC regeneration. Further investigation is needed to discover the subpopulations, cell PMRs, cellular and molecular recruitment mechanisms of ESPCs in vivo, and the behaviors and fates of the migrated ESPCs remain to be elucidated (A). More importantly, future studies should explore specific and potent chemoattractants that could achieve targeted ESPC recruitment without unwanted migration. In addition, the exploitation of appropriate chemoattractants, the definition of their dosage criteria, and the modification of their pharmacokinetics are also important issues to be addressed (B). It is also immensely crucial to develop advanced SDDSs that could be exploited for the stable and accurate spatiotemporal delivery of chemoattractants without the side effects (C). Moreover, gaining a deeper understanding of the interactions between biomimetic mechanical and biochemical stimuli and cartilage regeneration will provide new insights for in situ AC regeneration (D).

anchors.text: Figure 1. Different features of the osteochondral junction in normal and repair cartilage are revealed by hematoxylin and eosin (H & E) (A, C, E, G) and Safranin O/fast green/iron hematoxylin (SafO) (B, D, F, H). In normal human cartilage (A and B, adult hip surgical waste, femoral neck fracture), H&E clearly stains the tidemark (A, white arrows), while SafO readily discriminates cartilage from fast green-stained bone (below the black arrows, B). For heterogeneous human repair cartilage (C and D, biopsy taken 1 year postmicrofracture^{71,121}), H&E is better for determining the cartilage-bone boundary (black arrows, C) and abnormal mineralization (dashed circle), while SafO discriminates fibrocartilage from fast green-stained fibrous repair and bone (D). In hyaline cartilage repair elicited in a sheep model (E-H, 6 months posttreatment^{43}), the tidemark is beginning to form (white arrows, 10x magnification for E and F, 40x magnification for G and H). White arrows = tidemark; black arrows = cartilage-bone interface; AC = articular cartilage; cc = calcified cartilage; FC = fibrocartilage; HC = hyaline cartilage; b = bone.

Figure 2. Appearance of human 2-mm-diameter biopsy obtained with a Jamshidi 11-gauge needle (A, C) and corresponding decalcified Safranin O-stained paraffin section (B, D). Samples were obtained ex vivo with an ethics-approved protocol from the same lateral condyle (nonlesional area) obtained after total knee arthroplasty (74-year-old female). (A and B) A biopsy cored perpendicular to the surface and (C and D) a biopsy cored deliberately at an oblique angle to the surface are shown. Both biopsies were initially 6 mm long, but the subchondral bone was missing from the oblique biopsy prior to histoprocessing (C). Part of the subchondral bone in the perpendicular biopsy (B) was lost during histoprocessing.

Figure 3. Histoprocessing and histomorphometry of large animal defects. The example is taken from a sheep cartilage repair model (6 months repair $ ^{43} $). In this unilateral cartilage repair model, the repaired defect (top panels) was decalcified, trimmed at 2 levels in the defect (midproximal and middistal), and stained with Safranin O/Fast Green. Repair tissue above the projected tidemark was cropped using histomorphometric software, and total area (TA) and total stained repair tissue area (TS) were used to determine percentage of Safranin O-stained repair. The contralateral intact condyle was decalcified, trimmed through the middle, and cropped with matching defect width, and total area was used to determine percentage fill of the defect with repair tissue.

Figure 4. Example of standardized histoprocessing to evaluate a human biopsy (A-D, from cadaveric knee medial femoral condyle) or sheep hyaline repair cartilage 6-month repair after treatment with microfracture and chitosan-GP/blood implant (E-H). $ ^{43} $ Sections were stained for Safranin O, immunostained for collagen type II and collagen type I, and observed by polarized light microscopy (PLM). SZ = superficial zone; DZ = deep zone; AC = articular cartilage. Note the abnormal vascular invasion and mineralization (*) in this particular human biopsy above the tidemark (horizontal arrow, A-D), which is frequently observed in osteoarthritis. $ ^{21} $

Figure 5. Histomorphometry of chondral versus subchondral soft repair tissues. The example is from a 2-month repair of a trochlear full-thickness rabbit knee defect with two 0.9-mm microdrill holes. $ ^{44} $ (A) Safranin O-stained trochlear repair tissue, with the “projected tidemark” drawn through the defect area. (B) The chondral repair is cropped separately from the subchondral soft tissue repair for further histomorphometric analysis.

anchors.text: Fig. 1. Experimental design showing the protocol followed for all experiments. All cultures were grown for 7 days and were treated on the 8th day. For aggrecan and collagen experiments, cells were incubated in the absence or presence of signal transduction pathway inhibitors for 2 h prior to initiation of electrical stimulation at 60 kHz and 20 mV/cm (1 h at 50% duty cycle for aggrecan, gray box, and 6 h at 8.3% duty cycle for type II collagen, white box); samples were harvested 4 h and 6 h after initiation of electrical stimulation, respectively. For metalloproteinase experiments, cells were incubated in the absence or presence of signal transduction pathway inhibitors and/or IL-1β for 2 h prior to initiation of electrical stimulation (30 min at 100% duty cycle, black box); samples were harvested 22 h after initiation of electrical stimulation.

Fig. 2. Schematic diagram of relevant calcium signal transduction pathways showing the steps inhibited (indicated by a red ×) by the specific compounds tested. The main pathway of interest involves the opening of voltage-gated calcium channels (blocked by verapamil) by electrical stimulation, allowing the entry of extracellular Ca²⁺ resulting in elevated cytoplasmic Ca²⁺ levels. This results in activation of calmodulin (blocked by W-7) and the subsequent activation of calcineurin which dephosphorylates NF-AT (blocked by cyclosporin A). NF-AT then translocates to the nucleus where it acts in conjunction with other associated proteins as transcription factors. Another calcium-related pathway involves the conversion of PI₃₂ to IP₃ by the action of phospholipase C (blocked by neomycin) and the IP₃-induced release of intracellular Ca²⁺ stores to the cytoplasm (blocked by cyclosporin A and TMB-8). An increase in intracellular Ca²⁺ can also increase in PLA₂ activity (blocked by BB) leading to PGE₂ synthesis (blocked by indomethacin). IP₃R = inositol 1,4,5-triphosphate receptor, TF = any one or more generic transcription factors associated with NF-AT (Diagram adapted from Ref. 15).

Fig. 4. Effect of IL-1 $ \beta $ and/or signal transduction inhibitors on the regulation of MMP mRNA levels by electrical stimulation. For the groups labeled None, Neomycin, Verapamil and Cyclosporin, n = 12; for all other groups, n = 6. (A) MMP-1 expression. * denotes P < 0.0001, NS = not significant (P > 0.99); ** denotes unstimulated groups not significantly different from each other (P > 0.22); † denotes stimulated groups not significantly different from each other (P > 0.55). (B) MMP-3 expression. * denotes P < 0.0001, NS = not significant (P > 0.99); ** denotes unstimulated groups not significantly different from each other (P > 0.47); † denotes stimulated groups not significantly different from each other (P > 0.12). (C) MMP-13 expression. * denotes P < 0.0001, NS = not significant (P > 0.99); ** denotes unstimulated groups not significantly different from each other (P > 0.89). † denotes stimulated groups not significantly different from each other (P > 0.89).

Fig. 5. Effect of IL-1β and/or signal transduction inhibitors on the regulation of ADAMTS mRNA levels by electrical stimulation. For the groups labeled None, Neomycin, Verapamil and Cyclosporin, n=12; for all other groups, n=6. (A) ADAMTS-4 expression. * denotes P<0.0001, NS=not significant (P>0.98); ** denotes unstimulated groups not significantly different from each other (P>0.94); † denotes stimulated groups not significantly different from each other (P>0.69). (B) ADAMTS-5 expression. * denotes P<0.0001, NS=not significant (P>0.91); ** denotes unstimulated groups not significantly different from each other (P>0.95); † denotes stimulated groups not significantly different from each other (P=0.82).

Levels of IFN-γ, IL-2, and IL-4 in the supernatant or spienocytes harvested from the immunized S+H chickens after being cnaienged with the nignly virulent NDV strain F48E9 and IBV strain M41. A, B and C represent the levels of IFN-γ, IL-2, and IL-4 after being challenged with the NDV strain F48E9, respectively; D, E, and F represent levels of IFN-γ, IL-2, and IL-4 after being challenged with the IBV strain M41, respectively. The levels of IFN-γ, IL-2, and IL-4 in the supernatant were analyzed in an enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay for chicken IFN-γ, IL-2, and IL-4. anchors.text: Figure 1. The human body consists of various elastic, tough, and electroactive tissues under the action of a dynamic environment. The ideal tissue engineering scaffold therefore needs to satisfy a variety of mechanical and electrical demands to enable the generation of readily implemented tissue transplants.

Figure 2. A variety of approaches are currently being used to develop the much-needed multifunctional tissue engineering scaffolds. Nanoreinforced hydrogels stand as promising and convenient materials for this application given their range of properties including increased bioactivity, conductivity, and mechanical strength.

Figure 3. Engineering of an osteon-like, cell-laden hydrogel as discussed in Section 2.1. a) Schematic representation of the formation of hydroxyapatite nanoparticles in GelMA. b) Schematic representation of the UV-microfabrication procedure employed in the generation of the osteon-like microstructures. c) Bright-field and fluorescence imaging of the resulting biomimetic osteon construct. c) Reproduced with permission. $ ^{[54]} $ Copyright 2015, American Chemical Society.

Figure 4. Chemical structures of nanoclay platelets currently used for various biomedical engineering applications. Nanoclays are basically ultrathin ( $ \approx $1 nm thick) platelets with a dual charge that makes it easy to dissolve and incorporate into almost any existing hydrogel matrix.

Figure 5. A growth-factor-free solution $ ^{[15]} $ to bone-tissue engineering. a) Schematic representation of Laponite incorporation into GelMA. b) Mechanical data showing Laponite-facilitated reinforcement of GelMA, leading to a compressive Young's modulus nearly four times that of pure GelMA. c) In vitro osteogenic differentiation of preosteoblast cells as quantified by imaging of calcium (Alizarin Red S) and colorimetric analysis of the calcium concentration ( $ \times 10^{-6} $ M) in hydrogels containing different amounts of nanoparticles. Reproduced (adapted) with permission. $ ^{[15]} $ Copyright 2015, American Chemical Society.

Figure 6. A nanoreinforced and self-healing hydrogel. a,b) Schematic representation of the noncovalent and reversible bonding between hydroxyapatite nanoparticles and hyaluronan-bisphosphonate. c) Photographs showing the adhesion strength of the nanoreinforced hydroxyapatite-based hydrogel with mineralized PMMA and titanium implants. d) Quantitative data of the pull-off tests corresponding to the photographs in (c). Self-healing hybrid nanocomposites consisting of bisphosphonated hyaluronan and calcium phosphate nanoparticles, Reproduced with permission. $ ^{[139]} $ Copyright 2014, Elsevier.

Figure 7. Tissue-engineering applications of carbon-based nanocomposite hydrogels. Over the years, graphene sheets and CNTs have been used as nanofillers in hydrogels intended for use in neural, cardiac, and skeletal-muscle tissue engineering.

Figure 8. Gold-nanorod-based hydrogels for cardiac tissue engineering. a) Schematic representation of the fabrication process of hybrid nanocomposite hydrogels. b,c,d) The hybrid hydrogels displayed low impedance and almost 3-fold increase in Young's modulus as compared to pure GelMA hydrogels. e) The gold-nanorod-incorporated GelMA hydrogels promoted the expression of well-defined sarcomeric  $ \alpha $-actin in and a homogenous distribution of connexin-43. Reproduced with permission. $ ^{[163]} $ Copyright 2016, Elsevier.

Figure 9. Multilayered GO-based cellular-sheets for cardiac tissue engineering. a) Schematic representation of the layer-by-layer assembly onto GO-GelMA. b) Confocal images demonstrating the formation of a multilayered cell-sheet consisting of cardiac and endothelial cells. c) Cells in the multilayered tissue construct remained functional and viable after cell-layer exfoliation. d) The actuation was synchronous and could be controlled by the application of an electric field. Reproduced with permission. $ ^{[71]} $ Copyright 2014, Wiley-VCH.

Figure 10. GO-based hydrogels have been used as elastomeric and conductive fillers for skeletal muscle tissue engineering. a,b) GO incorporation into the hydrogel significantly improved the twisting and stretching properties of the hybrid gel. c,d) The hybrid gel could reconnect explanted abdominal muscle tissue from rats and enabled electrical conductance through the reconnected tissue. d) The threshold voltage for excitation of the reconnected muscle tissue dropped significantly in the presence of GO. Reproduced with permission. $ ^{[22]} $ Copyright 2016, Wiley-VCH.

Figure 11. CNTs have also been used as printable ink for 3D flexible electronics. a) Schematic illustrating the printing of conductive circuits from a CNT-based ink. b) 3D-printed CNT circuits embedded within a cell-laden GelMA hydrogel. c) 3D-encapsulated cardiac cells were healthy and expressing sarcomeric α-actinin after 10 d in culture and were not affected by the conductive CNT network. d) The 3D-printed construct could flex up to 115% of its initial length without breaking. e) The electrochemical activity was analyzed by impedance measurements and current–voltage curves. The measured capacitance (22.81 F g $ ^{-1} $) was higher than other CNT-based polymer composites, while the impedance was comparable to previously reported values. Reproduced with permission. $ ^{[265]} $ Copyright 2016, Wiley-VCH.

Figure 12. Merging nanoelectronics with living cells – a roadmap to a cyborganic future. a) Schematics of the fabrication procedure for silicon nanowires and an optical image showing the fibers and nanoelectronics in the hybrid scaffold. b) Confocal image of encapsulated cardiac cells expressing sarcomeric  $ \alpha $-actinin. c) Fluorescence imaging demonstrating the expected metabolic activity of the encapsulated cardiac cells. Moreover, electrical measurements showed that the conductance through the nanowires dropped significantly as noradrenaline was added to the hybrid scaffolds. d,e) Smooth-muscle cells were encapsulated within the hybrid scaffolds and folded into lumen-like structures. f) Histological staining of the generated lumen-like constructs demonstrated the formation of smooth muscle tissue (pink: haematoxylin–eosin staining, blue: Masson–Trichrome staining). Adapted with permission. $ ^{[288]} $ Copyright 2012, Macmillan Publishers Ltd.

Figure 13. Vertically aligned CNT microarrays inside GelMA can yield controlled and improved actuation of cardiac-based bioactuators. a) Schematic showing the concepts behind the fabrication of the hybrid bioactuator. b) Cardiac cells were healthy and expressing important markers. Cells within the dotted square were located between CNT electrodes, while cells within the dotted yellow square were located parallel to the CNT electrodes. d) An image of the free-standing hybrid actuator in culture media. f) A phase-contrast image showing the border region between the cultured cells and the CNT electrode array. g) The bioactuation could be tightly regulated by the applied electrical field. Reproduced with permission.[21] Copyright 2015, Wiley-VCH.

Figure 14. Emerging trends and future directions. a) 3D printing of hybrid neural circuits for neuron-to-machine interfaces. b) The potential application of cell-laden conductors in cyborganics. c) Use of 3D-printed neural circuits and cyborg skeletal muscle to generate advanced biorobots.

anchors.text: Fig. 1 The electrical cues in load-bearing soft tissues. On the left are examples of load-bearing soft tissues, including tendons, ligaments, and cartilage. In the center, two pathways for generating electrical signals within the tissue microenvironment are shown: the collagen piezoelectrical potential, produced by electric dipoles along the main stem of the triple helix structure, and the endogenous electrical signals generated by ion channels on the cell membrane. On the right, the functional effects of electrical signals are highlighted, influencing cell behaviors such as alignment, proliferation, and differentiation, as well as promoting tissue repair through processes like neovascularization and collagen synthesis (figures created with BioRender— https://www.biorender.com/).

Fig. 2 Working mechanism of electrical cues. This illustrates the influx of calcium ions and related signaling pathways triggered by electrical signals, which influence gene expression and cell behavior. anchors.text: Fig. 1. Multiple examination tests have been described to evaluating the rotator cuff. Tests for the supraspinatus include the empty can (Jobe) test (A) and the drop arm sign (B). The Jobe test is performed by abducting the arm in the plane of the scapula, internally rotating the shoulder and having the patient resist a downward force, and the drop arm sign is performed by passively elevating the arm in the scapular plane to the horizontal and asking the patient to slowly drop the arm. Both tests are positive if painful or weak. Tests for external rotation include the external rotation lag sign (C) and the Hornblower's sign (D). The external rotation lag sign is performed by passively externally rotating the shoulder with the elbow flexed to  $ 90^{\circ} $ and then asking the patient hold while letting go. This tests the infraspinatus and is positive if the arm drifts into internal rotation. The Hornblower's sign is performed by abducting and externally rotating the shoulder to  $ 90^{\circ} $ and asking the patient hold this position while letting go. This tests the teres minor and is positive if the arm drifts into internal rotation. Tests for the subscapularis include the belly press test (E), the bear hug test (F), and the lift off test (G). The belly press test is performed by asking the patient to press the palm into the abdomen and bring the elbow forward to the plane of the body. This can also be performed as a lag sign as demonstrated in the picture. The test is positive if weakness and inability to maintain the elbow in front of the plane of the body. The bear hug test is performed by placing the hand on the contralateral arm and asking the patient to resist while applying an anterior force. The test is positive with weakness or pain. The lift off test is performed by placing the patient's hand with the palm posterior on the lower back and asking the patient to lift the arm posteriorly off the back. This can also be performed as a lag sign as demonstrated in the figure. The test is positive if weakness and inability to move or keep the hand off the back.
Fig. 2. Examiner performs the Neer impingement test with the right arm stabilizing the scapula while passively raising the arm.
Fig. 3. Examiner performs the Hawkins test by passively applying an internal rotation force to the arm with  $ 90^{\circ} $ of forward flexion/abduction and the elbow flexed to  $ 90^{\circ} $.

Fig. 4. The Bigliani Classification of acromial morphology, demonstrating a Type I or flat acromion (A), a Type II or curved acromion (B), and a Type III or hooked acromion (C). (From Bright, A., Torpey, B., Magid, D. et al. Reliability of radiographic evaluation for acromial morphology. Skeletal Radiol 26, 718–721 (1997).)

Fig. 4. The Bigliani Classification of acromial morphology, demonstrating a Type I or flat acromion (A), a Type II or curved acromion (B), and a Type III or hooked acromion (C). (From Bright, A., Torpey, B., Magid, D. et al. Reliability of radiographic evaluation for acromial morphology. Skeletal Radiol 26, 718–721 (1997).)
Fig. 5. Example of the CSA measured as the angle of the glenoid plane from the inferior pole of the glenoid to the lateral edge of the acromion.

Fig. 6. Radiographic image of the sharpened lateral acromion morphology (A), with the ILAA measured at  $ 40^{\circ} $ (B), consistent with an SLAM sign. (From Amit P, Paluch AJ, Baring T. Sharpened lateral acromion morphology (SLAM sign) as an indicator of rotator cuff tear: a retrospective matched study. JSES Int. 2021 Jul 14;5(5):850-855. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jseint.2021.05.013. PMID: 34505095; PMCID: PMC8411071.)

Fig. 6. Radiographic image of the sharpened lateral acromion morphology (A), with the ILAA measured at  $ 40^{\circ} $ (B), consistent with an SLAM sign. (From Amit P, Paluch AJ, Baring T. Sharpened lateral acromion morphology (SLAM sign) as an indicator of rotator cuff tear: a retrospective matched study. JSES Int. 2021 Jul 14;5(5):850-855. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jseint.2021.05.013. PMID: 34505095; PMCID: PMC8411071.)

Fig. 7. Intraoperative arthroscopic view of the (A) posterior labrum fraying and the (B) articular side of the infraspinatus demonstrating fraying and degeneration in a patient with internal impingement. These are original images from the senior author.

Fig. 8. Examiner performs the posterior impingement test by placing the arm in  $ 90^{\circ} $ to  $ 110^{\circ} $ of abduction and maximally externally rotated to recreate the late cocking phase. The arm is then extended  $ 10^{\circ} $ to  $ 15^{\circ} $ and pain in this position is considered a positive test.
Fig. 9. Examiner performs the relocation sign by applying a posteriorly directed force on the proximal humerus, which should relieve pain.

Fig. 10. MRI arthrogram of the patient in Fig. 2, which demonstrates (A) fraying of the posterior labrum on an axial slice, as well as (B, C) a posterosuperior osseous cyst seen on the axial and coronal slices, as well as (D) degenerative tearing of the posterosuperior rotator cuff tissue.

Fig. 11. Examiner performs the coracoid impingement test by placing the shoulder passively in a position of cross-arm adduction, forward elevation, and internal rotation to bring the lesser tuberosity in contact with the coracoid. A positive test produces a painful clicking in the anterior shoulder.

Fig. 12. Axial MRI image showing subcoracoid impingement. The arrowhead depicts the subscapularis with intrasubstance tendinosis, and the arrow demonstrates the elongated coracoid and decreased coracohumeral distance. (From Freehill, Michael Q. MD. Coracoid Impingement: Diagnosis and Treatment. American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeon: April 2011 - Volume 19 - Issue 4 - p 191-197.)

anchors.text: Fig. 1 Experimental configuration and model of tetrapolar conductivity measurements. a) The tested sample is represented as two isotropic homogeneous layers of infinite lateral dimensions where layer 1 (with conductivity  $ \sigma_1 $) is the articular cartilage of thickness “d,” and layer 2 (with conductivity  $ \sigma_2 $) is the subchondral bone, taken to be of infinite thickness. There are three tetrapolar electrode configurations used in this study where the current is injected using one of three possible pairs of electrodes (#1–#8, #2–#7, #3–#6) while the potential difference is always measured by the central electrode pair (#4–#5). b) A light micrograph shows the 300  $ \mu $m regular spacing of the 8 electrodes of 50  $ \mu $m diameter. The faint circles above the electrodes are the nylon mesh in cross-section.

Fig. 2 Theoretical prediction and calibration of the apparent conductivity as function of the thickness of layer 1. a) The apparent conductivity (Eq. 2) for the three tetrapolar configurations as a function of the thickness of layer 1 (d), calculated using model assumptions explained in Fig. 1 and with $\sigma_1 = 1$ S/m, $\sigma_2 = 0.2$ S/m and $a = 300$ $\mu$m. The model predicts that the apparent conductivity approaches that of layer 1 when layer 1 thickness is $>2\times$ the inter-electrode spacing ($\sim600$ $\mu$m for equidistant configuration #3-#6) and approaches that of layer 2 when the thickness of layer 1 is $\sim10$ $\times$ less than the inter-electrode spacing ($\sim30$ $\mu$m for equidistant configuration #3-#6). Spacing apart the injection electrodes (using #2-#7, #1-#8) results in lower apparent conductivity due to deeper penetration of the current and therefore greater influence of the lower conductivity of layer 2. b) The apparent conductivity was measured using three different NaCl concentrations (0.03 M, 0.1 M, 0.5 M) with electrical conductivities ($\sigma_1$) of (0.34 S/m, 1.04 S/m, 4.54 S/m). The distance, $d$, between the upper post and chamber bottom was varied to change the thickness of the layer of known conductivity, $\sigma_1$, and measured apparent conductivity was normalized as $\sigma_{\text{app}} / \sigma_1$ shown in the figure. The $x$ axis in Figure 2b was shifted such that the point of contact was taken as 50 $\mu$m separation rather than 0 $\mu$m separation, due to non-parallelism of the two surfaces. The mean$\pm$sd of these three normalized conductivities (3 salt concentrations) are shown for each of the tetrapolar configurations (○ for #3-#6, ■ for #2-#7, △ for #1-#8) along with the theoretical prediction calculated using Eq. 3 with $\sigma_2 = 0$.

Fig. 3 Experimental apparatus for electrical conductivity measurement. a) Articular cartilage slices (2 mm wide, 12 mm long and 200-550  $ \mu $m thick) were positioned on the center of the microelectrode array and slightly compressed (5  $ \mu $m) under uniaxial unconfined compression geometry to assure good electrical contact. Electrical conductivity was measured using the equidistant electrode configuration with electrodes #3 and #6 injecting current. b) Electrical conductivity of disk-shaped samples (3.5 mm diameter with full-thickness articular cartilage attached to underlying bone) were measured by gluing the bone surface onto a transparent plastic plate that was then glued to a stainless steel bolt that was heavy enough (7.2 g) to ensure good contact when placing the articular cartilage surface in contact with the exposed electrodes. All three tetrapolar configurations were used to measure conductivity in this case. For both types of experiments, the test chamber was filled with 0.15 M phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) that has an electrical conductivity of 1.52 S/m. An alternating current of 1  $ \mu $A amplitude was injected at frequencies in the range of 10 Hz to 1000 Hz.

Fig. 4 Example raw data. a) Typical measured sinusoidal voltage for the equidistant tetrapolar configuration. b) Fourier-transformed raw data shows the ratio of the measured voltage to applied current, amplitude and phase (voltage-current) and total harmonic distortion (THD) as function of frequency.

Fig. 6 Apparent conductivity as a function of sample thickness for the three tetrapolar configurations (example data). The apparent conductivity of disk samples were obtained with the chamber of Fig. 3b. The cartilage thickness was reduced by removing slices consecutively with a vibratome and the sample thickness (cartilage+bone) was measured with a micrometer after each slice was removed. The apparent conductivity decreases with decreasing cartilage thickness, and when the injecting electrodes are farther apart, as predicted by the model (Fig. 2).

Fig. 7 Histological appearance of cartilage/bone disks with and without cutting to reduce cartilage thickness. Disk samples were matched as adjacent duplicates during isolation where one of each duplicate was used for conductivity measurements as a function of cartilage thickness (Fig. 3b) and then preserved by aldehyde fixation (B, D, F) while the other was chemically fixed directly without cutting (A,C,E). Disks were washed, embedded, sectioned and stained with toluidine blue. The last cut usually arrived just above the tidemark (B), however some uncalcified cartilage could remain (D). Variations in bone porosity and the thickness of the subchondral bone plate were evident (A and E to C). With respect to Table 2, B=sample 2, D=sample 5, F=sample 9. UC=uncalcified cartilage, CC=calcified cartilage. Scale bar =300 μm.

Fig. 8 Comparison of cartilage thickness measured by conductivity and by a micrometer plus histology for 4 example disks. Conductivity measurements were performed on each disk using all three tetrapolar configurations at each thickness. These 3 conductivity values (Type A data) were used as inputs to a fitting routine that minimized differences between the 3 conductivity values and Eq. 2 by fixing  $ \sigma_2 $ to either 0.2 S/m ( $ \odot $) or 0 S/m ( $ \square $) and varying  $ \sigma_1 $ and  $ d $. The resulting best fit thickness $ ^+ $ after each cut are shown compared to the thickness ( $ \triangle $) obtained by subtracting the bone thickness measured microscopically on the histological section from the total disk thickness (cartilage+bone) measured with a micrometer after removing each slice. The thickness values obtained from best fit conductivity measurements using  $ \sigma_2 = 0 $ S/m appeared to match histology/micrometer thickness values better than those obtained using  $ \sigma_2 = 0.2 $ S/m.

anchors.text: Figure 1 Schematic representation of loading regimes of articular cartilage. Dynamic compression of the extracellular matrix induces deformation of cells and matrix, hydrostatic pressure gradients, and interstitial fluid flow. Fluid convection and separation of counterions from the fixed charge groups of the proteoglycan constituents gives rise to electrical streaming potentials and currents. In contrast, tissue shear deformation of a poroelastic tissue does not induce volumetric changes, intratissue fluid flow, or pressure gradients.

Figure 2 (A) Unconfined compression of a cylindrical disk specimen, which has been modeled by an axisymmetric finite-element implementation (89). (B) The relative fluid velocity profile in the upper quadrant of A at the end of a 60-sec-constant-velocity, 25  $ \mu $m ramp compression of a 1-mm-thick disk that is 3 mm in diameter. (C) Current density profile at the end of the ramp compression (see 89 for details). (D) Axial strain profile predicted (89) for a statically compressed disk with depth-dependent equilibrium modulus (e.g. 92).

Figure 3 (A) $ ^{35} $S-Sulfate incorporation as a measure of proteoglycan synthesis in cartilage explants that were removed from culture at 2, 4, 8, 24, or 48 h after simultaneous exposure to 0 or 300 ng/ml of IGF-1 and were held at either 1.0-mm cut thickness or 0.65-mm compressed thickness (reproduced from 75, by permission of the publisher). (B) $ ^{3} $H-Proline radiolabel incorporation as a measure of total protein synthesis in cartilage disks during a 2-h label terminating at 2, 4, 16, 24, and 48 h after treatment with IGF-1 and/or imposition of a 2% sinusoidal strain at 0.1 Hz. Values are normalized to those of control disks [0 ng/ml IGF-1 with no compression (reproduced from 100, by permission of the publisher)].

Figure 4 Sulfate and proline radiolabel incorporation (for proteoglycan and total protein synthesis) in cartilage disks subjected to dynamic tissue shear strain of 1% amplitude at 0.1 Hz, compared with control disks maintained at the same static-offset compressed thickness but with no dynamic shear (reproduced from 101, by permission of the publisher).

Figure 5 Aggrecan and type-II collagen gene expression and biosynthesis in response to a static compression to 50% of cut thickness (reproduced from 92, by permission of the publisher). (A) mRNA levels were quantified and normalized to glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase (GAPDH) as a function of time after step compression. (B) Sulfate and proline radiolabel incorporation for PG and total protein synthesis as a function of time after step compression, normalized to values of free-swelling controls at 24 h (see 104 for details).

Figure 6 (A) Low and (B) high magnification of chondrocyte within a native cartilage tissue disk subjected to 20% axial static unconfined compression, fixed, and visualized by electron microscope. (B) Ordered, anisotropic morphology or rough endoplasmic reticulum during compression, compared with the more istropic, randomly ordered distribution in uncompressed controls (see 111 for details). (C) CHO cells showing green fluorescence protein-6-sulfotransferase fusion protein transfected into cells and localized within rough endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi apparatus, visualized by using two-photon fluorescence microscopy.

Fig. 5. Measurement of growth plate lengths and thickness of P-z, PH-z and Ht-z. A) Length of distal femur growth plates. B) Thickness of distal femur epiphyseal plate zones. (Fig. 2 continues on next page)

Fig. 2 (continued)—38-year-old man with small full-thickness tear in right supraspinatus tendon. Rotator cuff muscles and acromiohumeral distance are normal.

E, T1-weighted sagittal oblique image shows no fatty degeneration of supraspinatus (SSP) or subscapularis (SSC) muscle (Goutallier stage 0 [6]). Small amount of fatty degeneration (Goutallier stage 1) is present in infraspinatus (ISP) muscle. Normal supraspinatus muscle crosses tangent (dashed line), connecting superior borders of scapular spine and superior margin of coracoid ("tangent sign" absent).

[10]. An acromiohumeral distance ≤ 7 mm was proof of full-thickness tear of the rotator cuff. Therefore, ≤ 7 mm is the cutoff value for abnormal acromiohumeral distance.

Residual supraspinatus muscle does not cross tangent (dashed line) through superior borders of scapular spine or superior margin of coracoid ("tangent sign" present). anchors.text: Fig. 1. Selective labeling of Gdf5-expressing cells in Gdf5 $ ^{CreERT2} $ mice. At birth, Gdf5 $ ^{Cre} $;R26R $ ^{25Green} $ labeled cells are found throughout the joint, including within the articular cartilage (white arrow) and the putative secondary ossification center (yellow arrowhead) (A). After tamoxifen administration at E17.5, Gdf5 $ ^{CreERT2} $; R26R $ ^{tdTomato} $ labeled cells are less numerous, and more restricted towards the articular cartilage (white arrow) (B). Gdf5 $ ^{Cre} $;R26R $ ^{25Green} $ remain present in all joint tissues through 6 months of age, including within the secondary ossification center (yellow arrowhead, C) as well as the entire thickness of the articular cartilage (E). Gdf5 $ ^{CreERT2} $; R26R $ ^{tdTomato} $ labeled cells remain restricted primarily to the articular cartilage (white arrows, D–F).

Fig. 2. Cells with a Prg4+ lineage respond to articular cartilage injury. Safranin-O/Fast green staining of mature mouse femoral articular cartilage before (A) and 7 days (B) after creation of a full-thickness chondral defect at 12 weeks of age. After tamoxifen administration to Prg4 $ ^{CreERT2} $/R26R $ ^{tdTomato} $ mice at 1 month of age, labeled cells are found throughout the superficial layer of the articular cartilage (C). One week after injury, cells within the defect site (dotted line) are Prg4+, indicating that cells with a Prg4-expressing lineage participate in the acute injury response (D).
